title: NHL Preseason Betting in Canada: Value or Trap?
excerpt: NHL preseason games open the betting calendar for Canadians every September. Here is where the real value hides, and where the traps are waiting.
author: Jane Williams
bodyHtml:
September is the month Canadian hockey bettors have been waiting for since June. Training camps open, rosters get shuffled and the first exhibition games appear on the board. NHL preseason betting is one of the most misunderstood corners of the Canadian sports betting calendar — a stretch where sharp bettors quietly build a bankroll while casual punters give it straight back. The difference between those two groups is not luck. It is understanding what a preseason game actually is, and pricing it accordingly.

This guide breaks down how exhibition hockey markets work, why the numbers move the way they do, and how Canadians can approach these games without walking into the obvious traps.

Why NHL preseason betting is different from the regular season

An exhibition game is not a competitive contest in any meaningful sense. Coaches are not trying to win. They are evaluating prospects, managing minutes, testing line combinations and getting goaltenders back into game shape. A roster that looks like a contender on paper might dress six players who will be in the AHL by October.

That single fact changes everything about how you should bet these games. In the regular season, you are handicapping talent, form, rest and matchups. In the preseason, you are primarily handicapping who is actually playing. A team's logo tells you almost nothing. The lineup card tells you almost everything.

Sportsbooks know this too, which is why they treat preseason hockey with caution. Limits are lower, lines are posted later, and the pricing is often looser than you would see in October. That combination creates both the opportunity and the danger.

Where the genuine value hides

The bettors who profit in September are not the ones with better hockey opinions. They are the ones with better information, earlier.

Roster news is the whole edge

Beat reporters, team social accounts and morning-skate updates are your primary research tools. If you learn at 11am that a club is resting its top six forwards and starting a third-string goalie, and the line has not yet moved to reflect it, you have found the clearest edge available anywhere in hockey betting all year. Preseason lines respond to lineup news slowly because there is less money in the market forcing them to move.

Teams that take exhibition hockey seriously

Some organisations use the preseason as a genuine competitive audition, dressing near-full lineups and playing their veterans real minutes. Others treat every game as a glorified practice. These tendencies are reasonably consistent from year to year, and they are not always reflected in the price. Tracking which clubs ice their best available roster is one of the few forms of preseason handicapping that actually compounds.

Totals over sides

Preseason goaltending is frequently shaky. Backups and prospects take the crease, defensive systems have not been drilled, and penalty numbers can be inflated as coaches let physical players make an impression. That environment produces more goals than a tight regular-season game. It does not mean you blindly bet the over — books have adjusted — but totals are generally a more honest market than sides, where the price is dominated by brand-name bias.

The traps that catch Canadian bettors

For every genuine edge, there is a way to lose money faster than usual. The most common mistakes are:

  • Betting the logo. Backing a strong franchise because they were good last season, when the roster on the ice bears no resemblance to that team.
  • Ignoring the goalie situation. Many clubs split preseason games between two or three netminders, which makes both the moneyline and total far harder to price than bettors assume.
  • Overreacting to preseason results. A prospect scoring a hat trick in an exhibition game tells you very little about October. Do not let September performances contaminate your regular-season numbers.
  • Chasing volume. Because there is finally hockey on the board, bettors feel obliged to bet all of it. Preseason should be your lowest-volume, lowest-stake month of the year, not your highest.
  • Assuming stale lines are gifts. Sometimes a line looks wrong because the book has information you do not, particularly about late roster decisions.

Staking and bankroll in September

The single most important rule for preseason hockey is to size down. Whatever your standard unit is during the regular season, cut it. Variance in exhibition games is extreme — a single unexpected scratch or an early goaltender change can turn a well-reasoned bet into a coin flip. Treat September as a warm-up for your process, not a profit centre.

The other habit worth building before the season starts in earnest is line shopping. Preseason pricing varies more between books than at any other point in the hockey calendar, precisely because the markets are thin. Holding accounts at two or three operators lets you take the best available number on every play. Bettors in Alberta can see how the newer provincial market compares in our Alberta betting guide.

Using September to prepare for October

The best use of NHL preseason for most Canadian bettors is not betting it heavily at all. It is preparation. Use these few weeks to:

  • Open and verify accounts at multiple books so you are not stuck completing identity checks on opening night.
  • Test each platform's live-betting interface while stakes are small and the games do not matter.
  • Set your deposit limits and staking plan before the emotional pull of a real season kicks in.
  • Build the tracking spreadsheet you always mean to build and never do.
  • Watch camp battles so you know which young players have earned real roles by October.

That last point is where preseason genuinely pays. Bettors who follow training camps closely enter the regular season knowing which teams have solved their bottom-six problems and which are still patching holes. That knowledge is worth far more over 82 games than any exhibition wager.

Are preseason markets worth betting at all?

Honestly, for most people, only in small amounts. If you enjoy the games and want a modest stake to keep you engaged, preseason hockey is perfectly reasonable entertainment. If you are trying to build a season-long edge, your time is better spent on research than on action. The bettors who consistently beat exhibition markets are the ones plugged into beat-writer reporting in near real time, and that is a demanding way to earn a small return on low limits.

The middle path suits most Canadians well: bet lightly, focus on lineup-driven spots and totals, avoid the brand-name traps, and let September sharpen your process rather than drain your bankroll. If you are still getting comfortable with odds formats and bet types, our guide to sports betting basics is a good place to start before the puck drops for real.

The bottom line

NHL preseason betting is neither a goldmine nor a scam. It is a low-limit, information-driven market where the edge belongs to whoever reads the lineup news first and respects how little the final score actually means. Approach it with small stakes, sharp research and realistic expectations, and September becomes a useful runway into the season that matters.
